title: Private Deployments: VPC & On‑Prem Reference, Packaging, Day‑2 Ops, Upgrade & Rollback
author: Daniel Kim
body:
Overview

This document consolidates our recommended reference architectures, packaging and installation options, day-2 operational guidance, and approved upgrade and rollback procedures for Redwood Private deployments (VPC and on‑prem). It also captures the customer requirements library we use to qualify and plan deployments. Target audience: solutions engineers, customer SREs, and platform engineers responsible for onboarding and operating private deployments.

Scope

- VPC-hosted private control plane with customer-managed networking
- On‑prem appliance packaging and installation modalities
- Day‑2 operations (monitoring, backups, scaling, security hygiene)
- Upgrade and rollback procedures for control-plane and serving runtime
- Customer requirements and minimum hardware/network/security profile

Summary of recommended architectures

1) VPC (single-region, production)
- Components: Private control-plane (managed by Redwood or customer-hosted), dedicated GPU serving cluster, ingress gateway, metrics & logging stack, KMS integration, audit-log forwarding.
- Placement: Control plane in customer VPC with dedicated subnets (control-plane-subnet, serving-subnet, management-subnet). Serving nodes may run in the same VPC or a connected dedicated account depending on tenancy requirements.
- High-level diagram (text): Internet → Customer Load Balancer → Ingress Gateway → Control Plane / API services → Serving fleet (GPU nodes)

2) On‑prem (air‑gapped or rack-delivered appliance model)
- Components: Kubernetes (RKE/AKS/eksD supported variants), node pools for control-plane, serving, and logging/observability, local artifact registry (optional), KMS/HSM connector via appliance agent, and out-of-band telemetry relay where allowed.
- Packaging: Delivered as OCI images + Helm charts + preflight check tool. For air‑gapped installs we provide an offline bundle and install script.

Packaging and distribution options

- Online Helm package: recommended for most VPC and hybrid customers. Helm chart versioned with semver and SHA256 artifacts.
- Offline bundle: tar.gz containing helm charts, OCI images (manifest), upgrade manifests, and checksums. Used for strictly air‑gapped installs.
- Appliance ISO: for fully managed on‑prem racks; includes preconfigured OS image and installer.

Pre-deployment checklist (minimum required items)

| Item | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimum GPU profile | yes | 4 x A10G / 2 x A100 (or equivalent) for production serving cluster; scale by expected QPS |
| Control plane CPU/memory | yes | 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM (baseline; scale for multi-tenant control planes) |
| Network CIDR planning | yes | allocate subnets for control-plane, serving, and management; plan NAT/Egress rules |
| Persistent storage | yes | 1-5 TiB NVMe-backed for model artifacts and KV cache persistence depending on workload |
| KMS/HSM | recommended | customer-managed KMS with external key encryption policies |
| Logging/metrics retention | yes | 90 days recommended for audit logs; 30-90 days for metrics depending on plan |

Network and IAM requirements

- Ports and endpoints:
  - 443/TCP for control-plane API and ingress.
  - 22/TCP only for bootstrap access (disable after install).
  - 9090/9100 for Prometheus exporters (internal only).
  - 514/UDP or syslog TCP for audit log forwarding (optional).
- VPC routing: Ensure cross-AZ routing and NAT gateway access for pulling images (unless using offline bundle).
- IAM roles: minimum IAM role for control-plane to access image registry, KMS, and S3-compatible storage. Use least privilege policy templates in the appendix.

Installation and bootstrap (high-level steps)

1. Validate prerequisites using preflight tool (checks for DNS, IPAM, quotas, kernel modules).
2. Provision target infrastructure (VPC subnets, security groups, node pools).
3. Apply Helm chart (or offline installer) for control-plane in management namespace.
4. Register serving cluster with control-plane; run smoke tests (token auth, model ping).
5. Configure telemetry sinks: Prometheus scrape targets, Elasticsearch/S3 for logs, and KMS.

Day‑2 operations: monitoring, scaling, and maintenance

Monitoring & alerting
- Default SLOs: 99th percentile token latency < 250 ms for production small models; P99 token latency targets should be set per-model.
- Key alerts: GPU OOMs, high KV cache miss rate (>10%), control-plane API error rate > 1% sustained for 5m, node CPU throttling > 80% for 10m.
- Dashboards: per-model throughput/latency, per-route cost breakdown, and cluster-level GPU utilization.

Scaling considerations
- Horizontal serving scaling: scale GPU node pool according to model concurrency and batching profile. Autoscaling policy templates provided in the helm values (appendix).
- Batch tuning: Adjust batch size and batch latency budget to trade off throughput vs latency. Redwood Optimize recommendations can be applied to model-specific configs.

Backups and disaster recovery
- Control-plane state: daily snapshots to S3 or equivalent; retention 30 days by default.
- Model artifacts: versioned object store with immutability policy enabled.
- KV cache persistence: optional; if enabled, schedule hourly backups and verify restore procedure quarterly.

Maintenance windows and feature flags
- Use canary rollouts and blue/green deployments for control-plane and serving runtime updates.
- Default maintenance window: 02:00-06:00 local (customer) time unless otherwise agreed.

Upgrade and rollback procedures (control-plane and serving runtime)

Goals: zero data loss, predictable rollback path, and minimal serving disruption. Follow the steps below for minor and major upgrades.

Prerequisites before upgrade:
- Current snapshots of control-plane state stored off-cluster.
- Health checks passing for all control-plane components.
- Serving fleet at or below 60% utilization recommended.
- Test upgrade in a staging environment with representative traffic and model set.

Minor upgrade (patch/minor semver e.g., 1.4.x → 1.4.y):
1. Create a candidate bundle and verify SHA256 checksums.
2. Run control-plane upgrade on a single replica (canary) using helm upgrade --set canary=true.
3. Run smoke tests on control-plane API and user flows (login, model list, simple generate).
4. If canary is healthy for 30 minutes, roll out to remaining replicas with automated rolling update.
5. Upgrade serving runtime node pool in waves: drain one node, upgrade runtime agent, run model ping and throughput validation, then bring node back into rotation. Continue until complete.
6. Post-upgrade validation: compare pre/post SLO metrics, inspect logs for errors, and run a regression eval on 1000 sample prompts.

Rollback (minor)
- If the canary fails or post-upgrade validation shows regressions, immediately helm rollback to previous control-plane release on the canary replica and abort rollout. For serving runtime, revert to previous agent image and allow nodes to rejoin.

Major upgrade (semver bump or schema changes):
1. Read the release notes and migration guide; ensure all data migrations have reversible steps where possible.
2. Run the upgrade in a staging environment and exercise data migrations.
3. Schedule maintenance window and notify stakeholders 48 hours in advance.
4. Snapshot control plane and object storage.
5. Perform control-plane upgrade as canary, then full rollout after 1-2 hours of validated traffic.
6. Serving runtime upgrade as above, with extended monitoring and mandatory regression evals.

Rollback (major)
- If irreversible migrations were applied, follow the documented migration rollback procedure in the release notes. If not possible to rollback safely, execute the fail-open plan: keep previous serving runtime nodes active while quarantining problematic control-plane replicas; engage Redwood incident response and engineering oncall.

Operational runbook snippets (troubleshooting common failures)

1) Control-plane unhealthy (API 5xx responses)
- Check control-plane pod logs and restart counts.
- Verify database connectivity and object store health.
- If database primary is degraded, failover to standby per DB vendor docs.
- Escalation: oncall-eng-platform after 15 minutes if errors persist.

2) Serving node OOMs or GPU errors
- Isolate the node: cordon and drain.
- Inspect dmesg and container logs for OOM killer events or driver errors.
- If hardware fault suspected, remove node from the pool and replace.

3) High KV cache miss rate
- Validate cache eviction policy and memory limits.
- Increase cache size or add nodes to hosting pool; consult Redwood Optimize recommendations.

Customer requirements library (catalog of profiles)

Profile: Small / PoC
- Serving: 1 GPU (A10G) node pool, 2 vCPU control-plane, 32 GB RAM
- Storage: 500 GB SSD
- Network: 1 Gbps egress
- Use case: internal demos, early integration testing

Profile: Production (balanced)
- Serving: 4 x A10G or 2 x A100, autoscaled nodepool
- Control plane: 4 vCPU, 16-32 GB RAM with HA replicas
- Storage: 2-5 TiB NVMe for models and artifacts
- Network: 10 Gbps egress and intra-cluster 25 Gbps recommended
- Security: KMS integration, audit logging to SIEM

Profile: High-throughput / enterprise
- Serving: multi-node A100/GPU fabric, dedicated quantized model pool, separate low-latency pool for small models
- Control plane: 8+ vCPU, 64 GB RAM, multi-AZ placement
- Storage: 10+ TiB, lifecycle policy for model tiers
- Network: 25+ Gbps fabric, private peering to customer backbone

Compliance and security considerations

- Audit logging: all control-plane API calls must be logged with user, timestamp, and request metadata; forward to customer SIEM.
- Data residency: support for region-specific buckets and KMS keys; document full data flow for compliance review.
- Encryption: TLS1.2+ for in-transit; at-rest encryption using customer KMS where required.
- RBAC: use principle-of-least-privilege templates supplied in the appendix.

Roles and escalation matrix

- Deployment owner (customer or Redwood solutions engineer): responsible for overall coordination, runbooks, and maintenance scheduling.
- Customer SRE: day-to-day operations and primary responder for alerts.
- Redwood oncall (platform): escalation for control-plane product issues (contact via PagerDuty).
- Security escalation: Redwood security oncall for suspected compromise or audit incidents.

Appendix A — Example helm install (online)

helm repo add redwood https://charts.redwood.ai/stable
helm repo update
helm upgrade --install redwood-control-plane redwood/control-plane \
  --namespace redwood --create-namespace \
  --set image.tag=1.5.2 \
  --set ingress.host=controlplane.customer.example.com \
  --values values-production.yaml

Appendix B — Example offline bundle install (summary)

# Extract bundle and run installer
tar -xzf redwood-offline-bundle-1.5.2.tar.gz
cd redwood-offline-bundle-1.5.2
./install-offline.sh --target-namespace redwood --values values-offline.yaml

Appendix C — Sample minimal RBAC policy (IAM template)

# JSON IAM policy (summary)
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject","s3:PutObject"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::redwood-models-*/*"] },
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["kms:Encrypt","kms:Decrypt"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:kms:...:key/..." ] }
  ]
}

Appendix D — Contact list
